item.title: Case Study: Vishap on curl (cookie.c + http2.c)
item.description: Two production files from curl, nine findings, five CWE classes.
item.content:encoded:
We pointed Vishap at two files from curl: lib/cookie.c and lib/http2.c. Between them it reported nine findings across five CWE classes. None is a proven vulnerability — these are triage candidates — but the shape of the results is worth writing down.

lib/cookie.c — one critical​

The critical finding is a data race (CWE-362): remove_expired and storecookie mutate the shared cookie list without synchronisation visible in the file. Whether that is exploitable depends on a share-lock contract defined elsewhere — which is exactly why the report says REQUIRES_REVIEW rather than asserting a vulnerability.

Three further findings: a NUL byte ends validation early in invalid_octets (CWE-20), an out-of-bounds read when indexing the cookie pieces array (CWE-125), and a partially initialised cookie left behind on allocation failure (CWE-459).

lib/http2.c — error paths​

The HTTP/2 file produced five findings, all on error paths; the happy path looked correct. Return values of stream initialisers go unchecked (CWE-252), cf_h2_ctx_free assumes a partially initialised context (CWE-459), a reachable DEBUGASSERT(0) compiles out to a silent NULL in release builds (CWE-617), and two optional items: window-size desync after a failed submit (CWE-754) and an unwritten single-thread contract (CWE-362).

What the reports looked like​

Each analysis produced the same structure: findings with CWE and severity, a STRIDE model tied to those findings, three refactoring options with effort estimates, and an audit trail with both the analysed-slice hash and the original material hash.

For cookie.c the recommended option was contract-hardening: fix the three local defects in two to three days and leave the locking architecture alone until someone proves concurrent access matters. For http2.c the same — the three important findings are all "propagate the failure" changes, not redesigns.

Read the full case studies: cookie.c and http2.c.

The honest caveats​

  • No proof of concept was built; nothing was fuzzed.
  • The material was truncated, which limits confidence in control flow across the cut.
  • Heuristic LLM analysis produces false positives. Some of these nine may be wrong, and some may already be known to curl's maintainers.

We drafted a disclosure note to security@curl.se describing both files. It is not sent yet.

item.title: Vishap v6.3.0 — Next.js Dashboard
item.description: A Next.js dashboard, OpenTelemetry tracing, and multi-tenant isolation by default.
item.content:encoded:
v6.3.0 replaces the Streamlit prototype with a Next.js dashboard, adds OpenTelemetry tracing across the whole pipeline, and turns multi-tenant isolation into something the database enforces rather than something each query is expected to remember.

A real UI​

The new dashboard is Next.js 16 with Clerk authentication. It does three things the prototype could not: it shows a list of jobs with live status, it renders reports as formatted Markdown instead of a text blob, and it keeps a per-browser job history you can return to.

The analyse form takes a file or pasted material, submits the job, polls it, and redirects to the report when the pipeline finishes. Nothing else to learn.

Tracing you can follow​

Every analysis produces an OpenTelemetry trace: one span per pipeline stage, one for the Celery task, exported over OTLP to Tempo and readable in Grafana. When a job takes 40 seconds instead of 12, you can see which stage spent the time rather than guessing.

The instrumentation is fail-open. If OpenTelemetry is not installed or OTEL_SDK_DISABLED is set, the application runs exactly as before and the spans become no-ops. Tracing never becomes a startup dependency.

Multi-tenant isolation in the database​

Jobs are now isolated with PostgreSQL row-level security. Each request binds a tenant, and a policy restricts SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to rows belonging to that tenant — including the table owner, once FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is enabled. The application also sets the tenant on every session it opens, so a query that forgets to filter is still filtered.

This matters more than it sounds. Isolation that lives only in application code is one forgotten WHERE away from a cross-tenant leak. Isolation that lives in a policy is not.

The basics​

  • The job store is fully async, which fixed a real bug: the PostgreSQL backend's coroutines were never awaited, so async update paths silently did nothing.
  • The analysis history is tenant-scoped, including legacy rows with no tenant, which belong to public.
  • Audit-trail export is available as CSV or JSON for compliance collection.

Upgrade notes are in the documentation.

item.title: Vishap v6.3.1 — Multi-tenant RLS + Audit Export
item.description: Row-level security, audit export, GDPR endpoints, and two curl case studies.
item.content:encoded:
v6.3.1 is the release where isolation moved from application code into the database, and where the audit trail became something you can hand to an auditor instead of something you read in a dashboard.

Row-level security​

Jobs are now isolated by a PostgreSQL policy rather than by remembering to add a WHERE tenant_id = ... to every query. Every request binds a tenant, and the policy restricts SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to rows belonging to it. FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY extends that to the table owner, so a future migration script cannot quietly bypass it.

The application also sets the tenant on each session through set_config('app.current_tenant', ..., true), which means a query that forgets to filter is still filtered by the database. Two independent layers, one mistake required in each.

This release also fixed a real bug found while building it: the PostgreSQL job store is async, and its coroutines were never awaited. Async update paths returned a pending coroutine and silently did nothing. The store interface is now fully async end to end.

Audit export​

GET /audit/export?format=csv and ?format=json return the caller's job trail with filters for date range, status and limit. The CSV streams row by row; the JSON mirrors the same eight columns. Report bodies are deliberately excluded — an auditor wants to know who did what and when, not the contents of a report.

This is the artifact SOC 2 and ISO 27001 evidence collection actually asks for.

GDPR endpoints​

GET /api/me/data exports every job and history entry for the tenant; DELETE /api/me erases them. Both are scoped by tenant, and both require a Clerk session.

SSO is stubbed, on purpose​

GET /auth/sso/login and POST /auth/sso/callback answer 501 Not Implemented with a clear detail message. SAML requires the Clerk Enterprise tier; returning an explicit 501 is more useful to integrators than a fake redirect, and it documents the plan boundary in code.

Two case studies on curl​

We ran the analyser over lib/cookie.c and lib/http2.c from curl. Nine findings across five CWE classes, including a potential data race and a NUL bypass in cookie validation. None is a proof of concept, and the reports say so. Both are published, along with a draft disclosure note.

Fixed: MDX comments​

The documentation site has been failing to build since the legal pages landed: Docusaurus compiles .md as MDX, and MDX does not accept HTML comments. The mirrors now use the MDX comment syntax. If your own site mixes HTML comments into Markdown, this is the release that would have caught it for us.

item.title: Welcome to Vishap
item.description: Automated security analysis for code, configuration, specs, logs and data.
item.content:encoded:
Vishap is a SaaS platform for automated security analysis of engineering materials — source code, configuration files, specifications, logs and structured data. You give it a file; it returns a report you can act on.

Most security tooling forces a choice. Rule-based scanners are precise but blind to anything nobody wrote a rule for. A general-purpose chat model reads broadly but produces prose you cannot file as evidence. Vishap runs both and keeps the results separate: deterministic SAST/SCA findings on one side, model reasoning on the other, synthesised into one document.

Each report contains:

  • Findings mapped to CWE and OWASP Top 10, with severity and the function or file they point at.
  • A STRIDE threat model derived from those findings rather than from a generic checklist.
  • Refactoring options with effort estimates in days, so the report can go into planning as-is.
  • An audit trail with a SHA-256 hash of the analysed slice, the provenance commit, and PII-redaction flags.

The report is deliberately honest about confidence. When something looks wrong but cannot be proven from the material, it says so and asks for a human review instead of asserting a vulnerability. That is why reports end in REQUIRES_REVIEW more often than in a clean SAFE.

Vishap is available as a web app, a CLI, an HTTP API and a GitHub App. The CLI exits non-zero when a quality gate fails, so it drops into a CI pipeline without parsing output. The GitHub App comments on pull requests.

Start with the getting started guide, or read what came out when we pointed it at curl's production code.
